title: Phase 8 · Stage 24: Layers, a clock and ids
summary: Sort every type into Domain, Application and Infrastructure namespaces, and give the Library an injected clock and id generator so time and identity are under your control.

steps.title: Who may know about whom
body: Shelfwise is now over a thousand lines in one file, and every type can see every other. Real applications draw **layers**, each allowed to depend only on the ones beneath it:
| **Infrastructure** | `InMemoryRepository`, `FileSnapshotStore`, the fake lookup service, the clock | Domain, Application |
| **UI** (the top level) | parsing commands, printing | everything, and wires it together |

The sandbox allows one `Program.cs`, so the layers are **namespaces** in one file. Top-level statements must come first, so the namespaces go after them and the top of the file says `using Shelfwise.Domain;` and so on.

Two hidden dependencies remain inside the Library: it **owns the date** (`Today` with a private setter) and **counts ids itself** (`_members.Count + 1`). Both make the Library hard to test and wrong in a web server (where ids must be unique even after a restore). Make them interfaces:
interface IIdGenerator { int Next(string sequence); void Reset(string sequence, int last); }
class ManualClock(DateOnly start) : IClock          // Infrastructure: a clock you can move
public DateOnly Today { get; private set; } = start;
public void Advance(int days) => Today = Today.AddDays(days);
public void Set(DateOnly date) => Today = date;
The Library takes them in its constructor, like the repositories. The **composition root** (the top of `Program.cs`) is the only place that knows which concrete classes are used.

steps.prompt: Which layer does each type belong to?
steps.explain: Rules and values are Domain. Use cases and the interfaces they need are Application. Anything that touches files, memory stores or the outside world, and the concrete clock, is Infrastructure.

steps.prompt: Why should the `Library` ask for an `IClock` instead of calling `DateTime.Today`?
options: Tests (and simulations like `advance`) can set the date, so results are repeatable
So the Library can change the system clock
steps.explain: Anything the code reads from the outside world (time, randomness, ids, files) is easier to test when it is passed in. That is the whole point of dependency injection.

code: public void Reset(string sequence, int last) => _last[sequence] = last;
steps.explain: Each sequence counts on its own. An assignment is an expression whose value is what was assigned, so `Next` stores and returns in one line.

steps.title: Namespaces, IClock and IIdGenerator
prompt: 1. **Clock and ids.** Add `IClock`, `IIdGenerator`, `ManualClock` (from the card) and `SequentialIdGenerator` (from the predict step, implementing the interface).

2. **Library.** Its constructor becomes `Library(IClock clock, IIdGenerator ids, IRepository<Book, string> books, IRepository<Member, int> members, IRepository<Loan, int> loans)`. `Today` is read from the clock, `Advance` is gone, new members and loans take `ids.Next("member")` / `ids.Next("loan")`. `Restore` no longer sets the date; it resets both id sequences to the highest restored id (0 when there are none).

3. **Top level.** Create `var clock = new ManualClock(new DateOnly(2026, 3, 2));` and `var ids = new SequentialIdGenerator();` and pass them in. `ReminderService(Library library, ManualClock clock)` advances the clock. After a successful `load` or `restore`, call `clock.Set(...)` with the snapshot's date.

4. **Layers.** Wrap the types in three namespaces after the top-level code, using the table on the card: `namespace Shelfwise.Domain { ... }`, `Shelfwise.Application`, `Shelfwise.Infrastructure`. Add `using Shelfwise.Domain;` (and the other two) at the top.
5. New command `about`: `Shelfwise v1: clock ManualClock (2026-03-02), ids SequentialIdGenerator, 3 books, 2 members`. Add it to `help` after `today`.
Everything else prints exactly as before, including ids after a `load`.
